turns.doctor_question: Just before one of these episodes starts, do you feel an urge that you can’t resist?
turns.patient_response:
Okay, is this a joke? Seriously, doctor, is there a hidden camera in this office or something? Because you just asked me that. You literally just asked me if there's an urge, and the time before that, and the time before that! I just told you, like, thirty seconds ago, that there is absolutely no urge. 

I'm trying to be cooperative, I really am, because I came here for help, but I feel like you're just not listening to a single word coming out of my mouth. I don't know if this is some kind of psychiatric test where you try to make the patient mad to see how they react, or if you're just reading off a clipboard and ignoring my answers, but it's really upsetting me. I don't have an urge! I can't resist an urge that doesn't exist! 

I'm going to explain this one more time, okay? I'm going to lay it out with as much detail as I possibly can so we can please, please move on. What scared everyone at work—my manager, the other servers, the kitchen staff—is that I started freezing up in the middle of service, or just doing things completely out of order. I've been doing this job a long time, I know how the flow of a dinner rush works, but suddenly my brain just... derailed. 

Instead of closing checks like I was supposed to be doing, I was just standing by the soda station holding the cash drawer key and repeating table numbers. I had no reason to have that key! I wasn't at the register! But there I was, just glued to the floor by the Diet Coke, chanting "Table four, table seven, table nine" while my tables were waiting for their change. 

There was no little tickle in my brain telling me to walk over there. There was no irresistible urge that I was trying to fight off. It just happened. I was just suddenly doing everything out of order and freezing up. I really, really don't know how to make that any clearer for you. Do you have that written down now? No urge. Just freezing up. Please tell me you got it this time.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have any tics—like blinking, grimacing, shoulder shrugging, or throat clearing—when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, okay, a different question. Thank you. Um... no. No, I didn't have anything like that. 

I mean, I guess I bit my nails a little bit in elementary school if I was nervous about a spelling test or something, but that's just normal kid stuff, right? Not... not what you're talking about. I never had any weird blinking things, or making faces, or shrugging my shoulders over and over. I was actually a really calm, still kid. I took some ballet classes when I was like, eight or nine, and I was always very focused on my posture and exactly how I moved. My mom used to say I was almost too serious about it for my age. So I never had any twitches or throat clearing or anything that I couldn't control. 

And honestly, doctor, that's part of why this whole situation right now is so completely terrifying to me, and to my family, and to everyone who knows me. Because I've never had anything even close to this happen before. Growing up, through high school, even when I was taking some classes at the community college a few years back, my body always did exactly what I told it to do. I was always in the driver's seat. I never had these... these glitches where I just freeze up out of nowhere. 

So, no, looking back, there was absolutely nothing like that when I was a child. I was completely normal.

turns.doctor_question: Just before an episode starts, do you ever feel an irresistible urge that gets relieved when you do the movement or say the phrase?
turns.patient_response:
Doctor, are you... I'm sorry, I'm just trying to understand. Did you lose your place on your notepad? Because we literally just went over this, twice, right before you asked me about being a kid. I really, really don't know why you keep asking me about an urge. It's making me feel like you're not listening to a single word I'm saying, and it's honestly making my heart pound because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here. 

I will say it again, as clearly and with as much detail as I possibly can, because I really need you to write this down so we can move on. There is no urge. There is no relief. What scared everyone at work so badly—and I mean really scared them, my manager was practically in tears—is the fact that there's no warning at all. I just start freezing up right in the middle of service, or I start doing things completely out of order. 

Like, I'll be right in the middle of a massive dinner rush, tickets are flying, the kitchen is yelling, and instead of closing checks like I'm supposed to be doing, my brain just... stops working right. I end up standing all the way over by the soda station, just totally frozen. And I'm holding the cash drawer key for absolutely no reason, just standing there like a mannequin, repeating table numbers out loud. I don't feel an urge to hold the key! I don't feel a buildup of tension that makes me want to stand by the soda machine! It just happens, and I'm stuck there doing things in the completely wrong order while my tables are waiting for me. 

Please, please tell me you understand this time. No urges. Just freezing up and doing things out of order. Can we please talk about something else now?
